Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

the top has several pale rings and a cloudy patch, mostly toward the right side. one ring is about the size of a mug base and another is wider, maybe from a flowerpot. i can't tell if the cloudy patch is in the finish or below it, so please don't assume it will come out with one particular treatment. there are some shallow scratches along the front edge and a darker dent on the right corner. the finish looks warmer around the handles, which might just be grime from use. the handles are brass-colored metal, not solid brass as far as i know, and two of the drawer pulls have loose screws. the bottom rail has a little dust and webbing but i haven't seen active insects, fresh powder, or soft wood. i did notice a musty smell when i opened the bottom drawer; it fades if the drawer stays open for a while.

i want to keep the sideboard usable and retain its old character, not make it look brand new. i am okay with cleaning and small repairs, and i might consider refinishing the top if that's really what the condition calls for, but i don't want to strip the whole cabinet just to get an even color. my aunt said, “it was always the good piece in the dining room, so don't sand it into something else.” i took that to mean she cares about the existing wood and finish, though i can't say whether she meant that the original finish must stay untouched. please treat that as a preference to respect, not a technical instruction from a conservator.

there are a few things i haven't checked because i don't want to make damage worse. i haven't taken the doors or drawers off, tested the finish with alcohol or another solvent, or tried to tighten the loose pulls. i don't know whether the top is solid walnut, veneer, or a mix, and i can't see the underside without moving the sideboard away from the wall. the back panel looks like thin boards, but i don't know if it is original. the left door crack might be limited to the surface or it might go through the wood, and i don't know if the sticking drawer is swollen, misaligned, or rubbing on a runner. if any step depends on one of these unknowns, tell me what i should look for before doing that step, rather than treating a guess as a fact.

this is in a small rented apartment, on a wood floor, and i have to do the work indoors unless something can be carried to the shared courtyard. the sideboard is heavy enough that i can't move it by myself, and i don't want a plan that starts by hauling it outside. i can clear the top and pull out the drawers, but i would need another person to lift or tilt the cabinet. i have a soft brush, microfiber cloths, a vacuum with a brush attachment, a basic screwdriver set, and a small LED work light. i don't have a sander, clamps, spray equipment, or a workshop. i could borrow hand tools from the building maintenance person, but i would need to ask first. i have not bought any cleaner, wax, stain, shellac, glue, or replacement hardware.

please keep the result focused on this sideboard and the constraints above. include a short list of signs that mean i should pause rather than continue, such as evidence of active insects, a crack that is moving, loose veneer, or a finish that reacts unexpectedly, but don't say those signs are already there. include reasonable cautions about ventilation, protecting the apartment floor, and not mixing cleaning products, without turning it into a long general safety manual. end with a few specific questions i could answer after the initial inspection if those answers would change the next steps. i need a practical plan and decision points, not a diagnosis, a restoration result, or a claim that the sideboard is definitely from the 1940s.", "output": "Create a practical, beginner-friendly restoration plan for this particular walnut sideboard. Keep it usable and preserve its old character; do not assume it needs to look new or that the whole cabinet should be stripped. Treat my aunt’s preference—“it was always the good piece in the dining room, so don't sand it into something else.”—as a preference for respecting the existing wood and finish, not as a technical instruction from a conservator.

## Sideboard and current condition
The sideboard is about 148 cm wide, 46 cm deep and 82 cm high. It has three top drawers and two lower doors. I picked it up from my aunt’s garage. She thinks it was bought in the late 1940s, but this is only her recollection; I have found no label or date inside. There is a small brass-colored oval plate on the back with no readable writing.

The left door has a narrow vertical crack near its lower hinge. One drawer sticks during the last few centimetres of closing. The top has several pale rings and a cloudy patch, mainly on the right; one ring is about the size of a mug base and another is wider, possibly from a flowerpot. I don’t know whether the cloudiness is in the finish or below it. There are shallow scratches along the front edge and a darker dent on the right corner. The finish looks warmer around the handles, which may simply be grime. The brass-colored metal handles are not known to be solid brass, and two drawer-pull screws are loose. The bottom rail has dust and webbing, but I have not seen active insects, fresh powder or soft wood. The bottom drawer smelled musty when opened; the smell fades when it is left open.

## Constraints and unknowns
I have not removed the doors or drawers, tested the finish with alcohol or another solvent, or tightened the pulls. I don’t know whether the top is solid walnut, veneer or a mix. I cannot see the underside without moving the sideboard away from the wall. The back panel appears to be thin boards, but I don’t know whether it is original. The door crack may be superficial or may go through the wood. The drawer may be swollen, misaligned or rubbing on a runner. Where a step depends on any of these unknowns, explain what I should look for first rather than treating a guess as fact.

The sideboard is in a small rented apartment, on a wood floor. Work must be indoors unless an item can be carried to the shared courtyard. It is too heavy for me to move alone; I can clear the top and remove drawers, but need another person to lift or tilt the cabinet. I have a soft brush, microfiber cloths, a vacuum with a brush attachment, basic screwdrivers and a small LED work light. I have no sander, clamps, spray equipment or workshop. I could ask the building maintenance person to lend hand tools. I have not bought any cleaner, wax, stain, shellac, glue or replacement hardware.

## Requested plan
Give the steps in a sensible order for someone familiar with basic household repairs but new to cabinet restoration. Include an initial inspection, explain which observations are safe without disassembly and which checks should only be done gently, and identify when to stop and consult a furniture restorer. Do not provide a diagnosis or claim that the sideboard is definitely from the 1940s.

Include a numbered section covering these stages, in this order if practical: 1. preparing the room and documenting the current condition; 2. checking the finish, veneer, joints, crack and drawer movement; 3. gentle cleaning and deciding whether the pale rings and cloudy area need further treatment; 4. small repairs to the crack, pulls or drawer only if inspection supports them; 5. deciding whether refinishing is appropriate, especially on the top; and 6. final care and what to monitor afterward. You may change the order if there is a practical reason, but explain why.

Do not advise gluing, sanding, scraping or using a solvent unless you first explain what would justify that step and what risks to watch for. I do not need product brands or a specialist shopping list. If materials are needed, describe their type and purpose, and flag anything that could damage veneer or an older finish. Include a short list of signs that mean I should pause, such as active insects, a moving crack, loose veneer or a finish reacting unexpectedly; do not imply that any of these signs is already present. Include reasonable cautions about ventilation, protecting the apartment floor and not mixing cleaning products, without turning the plan into a general safety manual. I'm going through each item checking that the rewritten outputs preserve the original details and phrasing accurately—0303 keeps Sam's quote intact, 0305 swaps in "supplied material" appropriately, 0304's German terms look correct, and now I'm moving on to review the longer entry 0289.

Here I'm noticing some nuance gets lost: the user's hedge about not knowing whether the aunt meant the original finish must stay untouched isn't carried into the output, and the user's stated openness to refinishing the top if condition warrants it also seems to be dropped or only partially reflected.

The cloudy-patch caveat not to assume one particular treatment is also dropped, replaced with a narrower claim about not knowing if the cloudiness is in the finish or below it. I'm also catching a quantity shift — "two drawer pulls have loose screws" became "two drawer-pull screws are loose," which isn't quite the same thing — and the explicit preference against starting with hauling the item outside is missing entirely, even though the output addresses indoor work and the courtyard as a fallback. These all read as dropped constraints that should count against fidelity.

Moving on, 0307 looks byte-identical and passes, and 0311's and 0306's rewordings stay faithful to intent. For 0312, though, the output turns an ambiguous closing line into a direct question to the model ("What do you think makes a delivery feel worth it?") and drops the word "biggest" from "the biggest thing that makes a delivery feel worth it" — a meaningful lexical and framing change, so I'm marking this one as a fail too.
